abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for analyzing multi-layer interconnected networks, addressing a fundamental gap in network theory where traditional single-layer models fail to capture complex interdependencies in modern infrastructure systems. We develop a unified mathematical formalism that characterizes coupling mechanisms between network layers through tensor-based representations, enabling the simultaneous modeling of physical, logical, and social network relationships. The proposed framework establishes rigorous connectivity criteria and derives bounds on percolation thresholds across interconnected topologies, demonstrating that network reliability exhibits non-trivial coupling effects that cannot be predicted by isolated layer analysis. Our theoretical contributions include a comprehensive taxonomy of layer interactions, generalized graph-theoretic operators for multi-layer structures, and fundamental theorems relating layer-wise properties to emergent system behavior. We prove that synchronization dynamics and cascade failures in multi-layer networks follow distinct patterns from single-layer counterparts, establishing new research directions for network optimization. The framework's generality is validated through applications to transportation networks exhibiting multi-modal dependencies and communication systems with overlay architectures. This paradigm shift from single-layer to multi-layer network modeling represents a fundamental advancement in graph theory and opens new avenues for network design in interdependent infrastructure systems.

We present significant theoretical improvements to network reliability analysis by developing a unified approach that bridges the gap between terminal reliability and all-terminal reliability measures in large-scale networks. Traditional methods suffer from computational intractability for networks exceeding hundreds of nodes, limiting their practical applicability to real-world communication and transportation networks. Our approach introduces a novel decomposition technique based on network factorization and subgraph enumeration that reduces computational complexity from exponential to pseudo-polynomial for series-parallel structures. We establish new theoretical results connecting graph separators to reliability bounds, demonstrating that networks with bounded treewidth admit efficient exact reliability computation through dynamic programming on tree decompositions. The improved bounds are shown to be tight for commonly encountered network topologies, including grid graphs and hierarchical modular structures prevalent in modern network design. Furthermore, we extend the framework to capture probabilistic edge failures with non-identical failure probabilities, addressing a critical limitation of previous approaches that assumed homogeneous reliability characteristics. Computational experiments on benchmark instances from telecommunications infrastructure demonstrate that our method achieves orders-of-magnitude speedup compared to state-of-the-art reliability algorithms while maintaining exactness. These theoretical advances substantially expand the scope of tractable network reliability problems and provide practical tools for network optimization under uncertainty.

This paper presents NetFlow+, an innovative system architecture for adaptive network flow optimization that fundamentally reimagines routing algorithms for next-generation communication networks. Unlike traditional routing protocols that rely on static topological information and predetermined metrics, NetFlow+ employs a decentralized multi-agent framework where network nodes collaboratively learn optimal flow distribution through continuous feedback loops. The system architecture integrates real-time network monitoring, predictive traffic modeling, and adaptive path selection into a cohesive optimization engine that operates across multiple timescales. We design novel distributed algorithms for joint flow allocation and congestion control that achieve provably optimal performance in dynamic network environments with time-varying demands. The system's core innovation lies in its ability to simultaneously optimize for multiple quality-of-service metrics while maintaining network reliability under partial node or link failures. Implementation in software-defined networking environments demonstrates that NetFlow+ reduces average packet delay by 40% and improves network throughput by 35% compared to conventional shortest-path routing. The proposed paradigm shift toward learning-based, decentralized network flow optimization addresses fundamental limitations of traditional approaches and establishes a new design philosophy for communication networks in the era of edge computing and Internet of Things applications.

We introduce an enhanced system for large-scale network design optimization that significantly advances the state-of-the-art in combinatorial optimization for transportation networks. The proposed system addresses the computational challenges inherent in capacitated network design problems, where traditional integer programming approaches fail to scale to realistic problem sizes with thousands of nodes and arcs. Our system architecture combines a novel branch-and-price framework with sophisticated cutting-plane generation and hybrid heuristic decomposition to achieve substantial improvements in solution quality and computation time. Key innovations include a dynamic arc-generation mechanism that adaptively refines the network representation during optimization, and an improved label-setting algorithm for shortest path computation that leverages GPU acceleration for parallel evaluation of path candidates. We design an integrated preprocessing module that exploits problem-specific structure to tighten formulation bounds, reducing the linear programming relaxation gap by an average of 28% across benchmark instances. Computational results on transportation network design problems demonstrate that our system finds provably optimal or near-optimal solutions for instances previously considered intractable, with speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude relative to commercial solvers. The improved system enables practical optimization of real-world transportation networks with complex constraints including emission regulations and multi-modal connectivity requirements.
